query: AlCrFeNiSi belongs to a high-entropy-alloy family developed to combine properties that traditional single-principal-element alloys often cannot achieve simultaneously. Earlier research sought stable solid solutions and adjusted HEA compositions to target particular properties, but tradeoffs persisted: the CoCrFeMnNi system has limited wear and corrosion resistance, manganese can promote oxidation and oxide spallation, and cobalt-containing systems raise cost and processability concerns. Conventional bulk fabrication can cause compositional segregation during cooling, whereas mainstream metallic additive-manufacturing techniques can generate residual thermal stresses that impair mechanical performance and increase processing complexity. Given cobalt-free AlCrFeNiSi powder feedstock, what single intervention could improve mechanical integrity while limiting segregation, residual stress, and defect formation? State one hypothesis containing the intervention, its causal mechanism, a quantitative or directional outcome relative to conventionally fabricated AlCrFeNiSi, the processing and test boundaries of validity, the prior evidence supporting it, and a decisive experiment that could falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In-situ substrate preheating at 500–600°C during laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) of cobalt-free AlCrFeNiSi will reduce cooling gradients and slow solidification, thereby limiting compositional segregation, residual thermal stresses, and defect formation while enhancing mechanical integrity compared with conventionally processed parts.
generation.material_initial_state: Cobalt-free AlCrFeNiSi powder feedstock processed by conventional LPBF without substrate preheating, exhibiting significant compositional segregation, residual stresses, and defect formation due to rapid cooling.
generation.intervention: Implement in-situ substrate preheating to 500–600°C during the LPBF process along with an optimized scanning strategy.
generation.conditions: The intervention applies to LPBF fabrication of AlCrFeNiSi using controlled laser parameters and substrate preheating within the stated temperature range; mechanical and microstructural evaluations are conducted under standard tensile and microanalysis testing procedures, within the typical processing and testing boundaries of metallic additive manufacturing.
generation.structural_mediator: Reduced thermal gradients during solidification, leading to finer, more uniform microstructures with minimized segregation at grain boundaries and lower density of defects.
generation.mechanism: Preheating the substrate raises the base temperature, which slows down cooling rates during solidification. This lower thermal gradient minimizes rapid quenching, thereby reducing residual stresses and limiting compositional segregation as the alloy’s elements have more time to homogenize. In turn, this yields improved mechanical performance with reduced defect formation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to conventional LPBF processing without substrate preheating, the preheated samples are expected to exhibit lower residual stress levels, reduced microsegregation, diminished defect density, and improved mechanical integrity (e.g., enhanced yield strength and ductility). The directional improvement is anticipated, though the precise magnitude of improvement remains uncertain.
generation.baseline: LPBF fabricated AlCrFeNiSi without substrate preheating, which typically shows high cooling gradients, pronounced residual thermal stress, and noticeable compositional segregation.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis is valid for LPBF-processed cobalt-free AlCrFeNiSi within the defined substrate preheating temperature range (500–600°C) and under an optimized laser scanning strategy; it may not hold if processing conditions deviate significantly or if applied to alloys with substantially different thermal properties.
generation.uncertainty: The exact quantitative improvement in mechanical properties (e.g., yield strength increment or reduction in defect density) is not well defined and may depend on the precise energy input, scan strategy, and other machine parameters. There is also uncertainty regarding the interplay between preheating and potential phase transformations in the alloy.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of AlCrFeNiSi samples using LPBF: one with in-situ substrate preheating at 500–600°C and one without preheating. Ensure all other processing parameters (laser power, scan speed, etc.) are identical. Post-process and subject both sets to identical microstructural characterization and mechanical testing.
measurements: Residual stresses quantified by X-ray diffraction or hole-drilling methods.
Microstructural analysis (e.g., EBSD and EDS) to assess compositional segregation and defect density.
Mechanical testing including tensile tests (to compare yield strength, ultimate tensile strength, and ductility).
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the preheated samples do not show statistically significant reductions in residual stress, compositional segregation, and defect density or fail to improve or match the mechanical properties compared to the non-preheated samples, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Eutectic high-entropy alloys (EHEAs) exhibit excellent casting properties and comprehensive mechanical performance, making them suitable for fabricating spatial engineering components using additive manufacturing techniques. However, the rapid solidification process also leads to increased internal stress and reduced structural stability in the components. Therefore, this study focuses on the AlFeCoCrNi2.1 EHEA as the research subject, utilizing laser additive manufacturing to fabricate components and systematically investigating the influence of heat treatment processes on the microstructure and mechanical properties of the components. The research demonstrates that low-temperature heat treatment (700 °C and below) acts as a stress relief-annealing process for the components. The yield strength decreased from 1003.2 MPa to 742.1 MPa. At 900 °C heat treatment, the constraining effect between recrystallized grains and surrounding grains outweighs the dislocation release effect caused by recrystallization, resulting in an increase in dislocation density. Manufacturing processes have a strong influence on the mechanical properties of HEAs. It has been determined that the CoCrFeNi part produced by the hot-rolling process has a better yield and ultimate strength compared to the casted parts [,,,]. Additive manufacturing processes, such as Laser-Powder Bed Fusion (L-PBF), can improve the mechanical properties of high-entropy alloys due to their inherent unique processing characteristics. Specifically, the rapid solidification and repeated remelting associated with these techniques facilitate the formation of fine grains and numerous substructures with a high density of dislocations, thereby enhancing the yield strength compared to conventionally processed alloys. Brif et al. [] showed that the yield strength of the CoCrFeNi alloy produced by the powder bed fusion (PBF) process is twice, respectively, the treble of that alloy in as-cast condition, and Kuzminova [] showed in turn that the yield strength of alloys using L-PBF is twice than that of hot-rolled alloys. However, the thermal cycling and partial remelting experienced by previous layers can significantly increase the hot cracking susceptibility of superalloys [].
